title: Are Females More Resistant to Extreme Neuromuscular Fatigue?
authors: Temesi J, Arnal PJ, Rupp T, Feasson L, Cartier R, Gergele L, Verges S, Martin V, Millet GY
population: 20 experienced ultra-trail runners (10 female, 10 male, matched by percent of winning time by sex) in a 110 km race
findings: Maximal voluntary knee extensor torque fell more in males than females (-38% vs -29%, P = 0.006); plantar flexor torque loss was similar (-26% vs -31%).
Plantar flexor potentiated twitch amplitude fell more in males (-23% vs -8%, P = 0.010), indicating greater plantar flexor peripheral fatigue in males.

Central fatigue (voluntary activation by TMS and nerve stimulation) decreased similarly in both sexes; knee extensor peripheral fatigue and corticospinal excitability and inhibition changes were similar.
Authors suggest lower fatigue in females could partly explain better relative performance as race distance increases.
limitations: 20 finishers, performance-matched, one race; single post-race measurement with no recovery time course. Menstrual status and contraceptive use not reported in the abstract.
implications: No change to recovery or taper length can be justified from n = 20 single-race data; background for the ultra module only.
Schedule post-ultra recovery by the individual's symptoms and wearable readiness trends, not by sex.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (MSSE, 2015-07, first author Temesi). Numbers confirmed in Europe PMC abstract (PMID 25304334).
